prompt: What is the name of H2Se(aq)?

choices.why: That is its name when it isn't dissolved in water. The (aq) label makes it an acid.
An acid of hydrogen and just one other element takes the hydro- prefix.
An acid of hydrogen and one other element always ends in -ic acid; -ous comes from anions ending in -ite.

explanation: H2Se(aq) is made of hydrogen and only one other element, so its name is hydro- + the stem of the element + -ic acid: hydroselenic acid.

prompt: HCl is written without an (aq) label. What is its name?

choices.why: That name is for HCl(aq), dissolved in water. Without the (aq) label, HCl is treated as a molecular compound.
Chloric acid is HClO3(aq), from the chlorate ion.

explanation: The (aq) label shows that a compound is dissolved in water. Without it, HCl is treated as a molecular compound, hydrogen chloride; dissolved in water, it is hydrochloric acid.

prompt: The chlorite ion is ClO2−. What is the name of HClO2(aq)?

choices.why: -ic acid comes from an anion ending in -ate: chlorate, ClO3−, gives chloric acid.
The hydro- prefix is only for acids of hydrogen and one other element. This acid contains a polyatomic ion.
The anion's ending changes: -ite becomes -ous acid.

explanation: An acid made from a polyatomic anion takes its name from the anion's stem. Chlorite ends in -ite, so the acid is chlor- + -ous acid: chlorous acid.

prompt: The carbonate ion is CO3^2−. What is the formula of carbonic acid?

choices.why: Carbonate has a 2− charge, so it takes two H+ ions to balance it.
The acid keeps the whole carbonate ion, CO3, so there are three oxygen atoms.

explanation: Carbonate ends in -ate, so its acid is carbonic acid. The acid is H+ ions with the carbonate ion, and CO3^2− needs two H+ to balance its charge: H2CO3(aq).

prompt: Which of these is a property of acids?

choices.text: Many react with some metals to form oxygen gas
choices.why: Acids that react with metals form metal ions and elemental hydrogen, not oxygen.

choices.text: They are rarely found in foods
choices.why: Acids are common in foods: citrus fruits, vinegar, spinach, and some soft drinks all contain them.

explanation: Acids taste sour (the sourness of citrus fruits and vinegar comes from acids), many react with some metals to form metal ions and hydrogen, and they change the colors of certain plant pigments.

prompt: Which acid is found in spinach and other green leafy vegetables?

choices.why: Citric acid is in citrus fruits.
Phosphoric acid is an ingredient in some soft drinks.
Hydrochloric acid is stomach acid, and it's also sold as a cleaner for concrete and masonry.

explanation: Oxalic acid, H2C2O4(aq), is found in spinach and other green leafy vegetables.

prompt: How does this section first define an acid?

choices.text: An ionic compound of the H+ cation dissolved in water
Any compound whose formula contains hydrogen
choices.why: Containing hydrogen isn't enough. The compound must have H+ as its cation, and it must be dissolved in water.

choices.text: An ionic compound of the OH− anion dissolved in water
choices.why: OH− is the hydroxide anion. The section defines an acid by its cation, H+.

choices.text: A molecular compound of hydrogen and a nonmetal
choices.why: That is how a formula without the (aq) label is treated. Dissolved in water, such a compound is treated as an acid.

explanation: The section initially defines an acid as an ionic compound of the H+ cation dissolved in water. The phase label (aq) after a formula shows that it is dissolved in water.

prompt: What does the phase label (aq) written after a chemical formula mean?

choices.text: The substance is dissolved in water.

choices.why: (aq) means only that the substance is dissolved in water. A dissolved compound is an acid only if its cation is H+.

choices.text: The substance is a molecular compound.
choices.why: It's the other way around: a formula without the (aq) label is treated as a molecular compound.

choices.text: The substance is a pure liquid.
choices.why: aq stands for aqueous, which describes something dissolved in water, not a pure substance.

explanation: The label (aq) stands for aqueous, a word that describes something dissolved in water. Any dissolved substance can carry it, so a compound with (aq) is an acid only if its cation is H+.

prompt: Which of these is an acid, as this section defines acids?

choices.why: Without the (aq) label, HF isn't shown as dissolved in water, so it is treated as a molecular compound, hydrogen fluoride.
It is dissolved in water, but its cation is Na+, not H+.
Its hydrogen atoms are part of the ammonium ion, NH4+. An acid's cation must be H+.

explanation: An acid is an ionic compound of the H+ cation dissolved in water. Only HF(aq) has H+ as its cation and carries the (aq) label.

prompt: Sodium bicarbonate, NaHCO3, contains hydrogen. Why is NaHCO3(aq) not an acid, as this section defines acids?

choices.text: Its cation is Na+; the hydrogen is part of the HCO3− anion.
It is not dissolved in water.
choices.why: The (aq) label shows that it is dissolved in water. The problem is that its cation is Na+, not H+.
Many acids, such as carbonic acid, H2CO3(aq), contain polyatomic anions. What matters is that the cation is H+.

choices.text: It has only one hydrogen atom.
choices.why: The number of hydrogen atoms doesn't decide it; many acids have just one H+. The hydrogen must be the cation, H+.

explanation: An acid is an ionic compound of the H+ cation dissolved in water. NaHCO3(aq) is dissolved in water, but its cation is Na+; its hydrogen is part of the bicarbonate ion, HCO3−.

prompt: In acid formulas such as H3PO4(aq), why is hydrogen written first?

choices.text: H+ is the cation, and ionic formulas list the cation first.
Hydrogen is the lightest element, so it always goes first.
choices.why: Ionic formulas aren't ordered by mass. The cation is written first, and in an acid the cation is H+.

choices.text: The acid's name begins with hydro-, so H goes first.
choices.why: Phosphoric acid has no hydro- prefix, yet H is still written first, because H+ is the cation.

choices.text: Hydrogen is the anion, and anions are written first.
choices.why: In an acid, hydrogen is the cation, H+. Ionic formulas list the cation first and the anion second.

explanation: The section defines an acid as an ionic compound of the H+ cation. Ionic formulas are written with the cation first and the anion second, so the H+ comes before the anion.

prompt: Phosphoric acid is H3PO4(aq). As this section defines acids, which ions make it up?

choices.text: Three H+ ions and one PO4^3− ion
One H3^3+ ion and one PO4^3− ion
choices.why: Each hydrogen is a separate H+ ion. The subscript 3 shows that three H+ ions balance the 3− charge of phosphate.

choices.text: Three H+ ions, one P^3− ion, and four O^2− ions
choices.why: Phosphate, PO4^3−, is a polyatomic ion, so its phosphorus and oxygen atoms stay together as one anion.

choices.text: Three H− ions and one PO4^3+ ion
choices.why: In an acid, hydrogen is the cation, H+, and phosphate is an anion, PO4^3−.

explanation: An acid is an ionic compound of the H+ cation. In H3PO4(aq), the anion is phosphate, PO4^3−, and three H+ ions balance its 3− charge.

prompt: The formula HC2H3O2(aq) has four hydrogen atoms. As this section defines acids, how many of them are H+ ions?

choices.why: The three hydrogens written inside C2H3O2 belong to the acetate ion, C2H3O2−. They aren't H+ ions.
Only the hydrogen written first is an H+ ion. The other three are part of the polyatomic acetate ion.
As the section defines it, every acid contains the H+ cation. Here it is the hydrogen written first.

explanation: HC2H3O2(aq) is H+ with the acetate ion, C2H3O2−. The anion's 1− charge is balanced by one H+, and the other three hydrogens are part of the acetate ion.

prompt: A piece of zinc metal reacts with an acid. According to this section, what forms?

choices.why: Acids that react with metals form metal ions and elemental hydrogen, not oxygen.
Metals form cations, not anions. Zinc forms the Zn^2+ ion.
That's backward. The reaction forms metal ions and elemental hydrogen, so zinc ends up as ions and hydrogen as the element.

explanation: Many acids react with some metallic elements to form metal ions and elemental hydrogen. Zinc forms the Zn^2+ cation, so the products are Zn^2+ ions and elemental hydrogen.

prompt: According to the section, what causes the ripening of some fruits and vegetables?

choices.text: The formation or destruction of excess acid in the plant
The conversion of plant pigments into acids
choices.why: Acids make certain plant pigments change colors; the section doesn't say the pigments become acids.

choices.text: The dissolving of the plant's acids in water
choices.why: Being dissolved in water is part of the definition of an acid. Ripening is tied to forming or destroying excess acid in the plant.

choices.text: The absorption of acids from the soil
choices.why: The section says the excess acid forms or is destroyed in the plant itself.

explanation: Acids make certain plant pigments change colors. Indeed, the ripening of some fruits and vegetables is caused by the formation or destruction of excess acid in the plant.

prompt: Which acid does the section say is found in the stomach and is also sold in hardware stores as a cleaner for concrete and masonry?

choices.why: Chloric acid comes from the chlorate ion. Stomach acid is hydrochloric acid.
Citric acid is found in citrus fruits.
Phosphoric acid is an ingredient in some soft drinks.

explanation: Hydrochloric acid, HCl(aq), is found in the stomach (stomach acid), and it can also be bought in hardware stores as a cleaner for concrete and masonry.

prompt: Which acids have names that begin with the prefix hydro-?

choices.text: Acids made of hydrogen and only one other element
Every acid, since every acid contains hydrogen
choices.why: Only acids of hydrogen and one other element take hydro-. Acids made from polyatomic anions don't.

choices.text: Acids made from an anion whose name ends in -ate
choices.why: These are named with the stem of the anion name plus -ic acid, with no hydro-.

choices.text: Acids made from an anion whose name ends in -ite
choices.why: These are named with the stem of the anion name plus -ous acid, with no hydro-.

explanation: If an acid is composed of only hydrogen and one other element, its name is hydro- + the stem of the other element + -ic acid, as in hydrochloric acid, HCl(aq).

prompt: Which of these acids has a name that begins with hydro-?

choices.why: It contains carbon and oxygen as well as hydrogen. Its name comes from the carbonate ion, with no hydro-.
It contains carbon and oxygen as well as hydrogen, so it isn't an acid of hydrogen and one other element.
It contains phosphorus and oxygen as well as hydrogen. Its name comes from the phosphate ion, with no hydro-.

explanation: Only an acid of hydrogen and one other element takes hydro-. HBr(aq) contains only hydrogen and bromine, so it is hydro- + brom + -ic acid: hydrobromic acid.

prompt: What is the formula of hydriodic acid?

choices.why: The iodide ion, I−, has a 1− charge, so one H+ balances it.
I3− is the triiodide ion. Hydriodic acid is made from H+ and the iodide ion, I−.
The hydro- prefix means the acid contains hydrogen and only one other element, so there is no oxygen.

explanation: The hydro- prefix means hydriodic acid contains only hydrogen and iodine. The iodide ion, I−, has a 1− charge, so one H+ balances it: HI(aq).

prompt: Hydrosulfuric acid and sulfuric acid have similar names. What are their formulas, in that order?

choices.why: These are reversed. The hydro- prefix marks the acid of hydrogen and sulfur only.
The sulfide ion, S^2−, has a 2− charge, so it takes two H+ ions.
The sulfate ion, SO4^2−, has a 2− charge, so it takes two H+ ions.

explanation: Hydrosulfuric acid is hydrogen and sulfur only; sulfide, S^2−, needs two H+: H2S(aq). Sulfuric acid comes from sulfate, SO4^2−, which also needs two H+: H2SO4(aq).

prompt: An acid is made from H+ ions and a polyatomic anion whose name ends in -ite. How is the acid named?

choices.text: The stem of the anion name + -ous acid
The stem of the anion name + -ic acid
choices.why: -ic acid comes from an anion whose name ends in -ate.

choices.text: Hydro- + the stem of the anion name + -ic acid
choices.why: Hydro- is only for acids of hydrogen and one other element, not acids of polyatomic anions.
The anion's ending changes in the acid's name: -ite becomes -ous.

explanation: If the anion's name ends in -ite, the acid's name is the stem of the anion name plus -ous acid. If it ends in -ate, the acid's name ends in -ic acid instead.

prompt: An acid's name ends in -ic acid and has no hydro- prefix. What does that tell you about the anion it is made from?

choices.text: It is a polyatomic anion whose name ends in -ate.
It is a polyatomic anion whose name ends in -ite.
choices.why: An anion ending in -ite gives an acid ending in -ous acid.

choices.text: It is a monatomic anion whose name ends in -ide.
choices.why: An acid of hydrogen and one other element, such as hydrochloric acid, takes the hydro- prefix.

choices.text: It is an anion that contains no oxygen atoms.
choices.why: The -ate anions, such as carbonate, CO3^2−, and sulfate, SO4^2−, contain oxygen.

explanation: Acids of hydrogen and one other element take hydro-, and -ite anions give -ous acids. So an -ic acid without hydro- comes from an anion ending in -ate, as carbonic acid comes from carbonate.

prompt: What is the name of the acid made from H+ ions and the anion in Na2SO3?

choices.why: -ic acid comes from an anion ending in -ate. SO3^2− is sulfite, which ends in -ite.
Hydro- is only for acids of hydrogen and one other element. This acid contains a polyatomic anion.
The anion's ending changes in the acid's name: -ite becomes -ous.

explanation: Na2SO3 is two Na+ ions with one sulfite ion, SO3^2−. Sulfite ends in -ite, so the acid is the stem plus -ous acid: sulfurous acid, H2SO3(aq).

prompt: What is the formula of perchloric acid?

choices.why: ClO3− is chlorate. The per- in perchloric acid comes from the perchlorate ion, ClO4−.
The perchlorate ion, ClO4−, has a 1− charge, so one H+ balances it.
An -ic acid with no hydro- prefix comes from a polyatomic anion, not from chloride.

explanation: Perchloric acid has no hydro- prefix and ends in -ic acid, so it comes from the -ate ion perchlorate, ClO4−. One H+ balances its 1− charge: HClO4(aq).

prompt: Which naming rule gives the name of HC2H3O2(aq)?

choices.text: Polyatomic anion ending in -ate: stem + -ic acid
Hydrogen and one other element: hydro- + stem + -ic acid
choices.why: The formula has carbon and oxygen as well as hydrogen, so it isn't an acid of hydrogen and one other element.

choices.text: Polyatomic anion ending in -ite: stem + -ous acid
choices.why: The anion is acetate, C2H3O2−, which ends in -ate, not -ite.

choices.text: Ionic compound naming: cation name + anion name
choices.why: With the (aq) label, the compound is an acid, and acids have their own naming system.

explanation: HC2H3O2(aq) is H+ with the polyatomic acetate ion, C2H3O2−. Acetate ends in -ate, so the acid's name is the stem plus -ic acid: acetic acid.

prompt: A student names H2CrO4(aq) "hydrochromic acid." What is wrong with this name?

choices.text: It has a polyatomic anion, so no hydro-; it is chromic acid.
The ending should be -ous; it is hydrochromous acid.
choices.why: Chromate, CrO4^2−, ends in -ate, which gives -ic acid, and hydro- doesn't belong.

choices.text: The name must count hydrogens; it is dihydrochromic acid.
choices.why: Acid names don't count hydrogen atoms. The anion's charge sets how many H+ ions there are.

choices.text: With (aq), it is named hydrogen chromate instead.
choices.why: The (aq) label means the compound is dissolved in water, so it is named as an acid.

explanation: H2CrO4(aq) is H+ with the polyatomic chromate ion, CrO4^2−, so its name has no hydro- prefix. Chromate ends in -ate, so the acid is chromic acid.

prompt: What is the formula of dichromic acid?

choices.why: The dichromate ion, Cr2O7^2−, has a 2− charge, so it takes two H+ ions.
CrO4^2− is chromate. Dichromic acid comes from the dichromate ion, Cr2O7^2−.
Dichromate is its own ion, Cr2O7^2−, not two chromate ions. The di- is part of the ion's name.

explanation: Dichromic acid comes from the dichromate ion, Cr2O7^2−; the di- stays because it is part of the ion's name. Two H+ ions balance its 2− charge: H2Cr2O7(aq).

prompt: Oxalic acid is H2C2O4(aq). What is the formula of the oxalate ion?

choices.why: There are two H+ ions, so the anion's charge must be 2− to balance them.
The H+ ions are separate cations; they aren't part of the anion.
In an acid, H+ is the cation, so oxalate must be an anion with a negative charge.

explanation: As the section defines acids, H2C2O4(aq) is two H+ ions with one anion. The two 1+ charges must be balanced, so the oxalate ion is C2O4^2−.

prompt: How does the formula of nitrous acid differ from the formula of nitric acid?

choices.text: It has one fewer oxygen atom and the same number of hydrogen atoms.
It has one more oxygen atom and the same number of hydrogen atoms.
choices.why: Nitrous acid comes from nitrite, which has one less oxygen than nitrate, not one more.

choices.text: It has one more hydrogen atom and the same number of oxygen atoms.
choices.why: -ous and -ic acids don't differ by a hydrogen. Nitrite and nitrate have the same 1− charge, so each acid has one H+.

choices.text: It has no oxygen atoms, because it comes from the nitride ion.
choices.why: An acid of hydrogen and one other element would take the hydro- prefix. Nitrous acid comes from nitrite, NO2−.

explanation: Nitric acid comes from nitrate, NO3−, and nitrous acid comes from nitrite, NO2−. Nitrite has one less oxygen and the same 1− charge, so the formulas are HNO3(aq) and HNO2(aq).

prompt: A student names HClO3(aq) "chlorous acid." What is the mistake?

choices.text: ClO3− is chlorate, so the acid is chloric acid.
ClO3− is perchlorate, so the acid is perchloric acid.
choices.why: Perchlorate is ClO4−, with four oxygen atoms. ClO3− is chlorate.

choices.text: The name is right, because ClO3− is chlorite.
choices.why: ClO3− is chlorate. Chlorite has one less oxygen: ClO2−.

choices.text: Hydro- is missing; the acid is hydrochlorous acid.
choices.why: Hydro- is only for acids of hydrogen and one other element, and an -ate ion gives an -ic acid.

explanation: ClO3− is the chlorate ion; chlorite, ClO2−, has one less oxygen. Chlorate ends in -ate, so HClO3(aq) is chloric acid.
